title: Kota Students Form 'Laddu Janta Party' After Promised Diwali Sweets Go Missing
excerpt: Allen Career Institute students say six promised laddus each never arrived before the Diwali break. Two days of slogans, placards and an Instagram party later, distribution reportedly began.
body:
• Students at Allen Career Institute in Kota say they were promised six laddus each before the Diwali break and did not receive them, The Times of India reported.
  • Students gathered outside Allen branches including Coral Park and Supath, raised slogans for about two days, and set up an Instagram page under the name Laddu Janta Party.
  • Allen director Brajesh Maheshwari reportedly said a surge in demand for sweets made it hard to arrange enough halwais in time.
  • Distribution reportedly began on November 5 after the protests, and other coaching institutes held a bhandara for students on Sunday, November 8.

Kota is used to student protests about exams, fees and pressure. This month it got one about sweets. Thousands of students at Allen Career Institute, the coaching chain that fills the Rajasthan city with JEE and NEET aspirants, say they were promised six laddus each before the Diwali break — and that the boxes never arrived, The Times of India reported.

How a missing sweet became a movement

Distributing sweets before the Diwali break is an Allen tradition, and students said they expected their share before leaving Kota for the holiday, which began around November 5. When the promised boxes reportedly did not reach several students, groups began gathering outside Allen branches, including in the Coral Park and Supath areas, after classes. The protests reportedly continued for around two days, with slogans and placards, and students say the crowds grew large enough that local management called in the police to manage the situation, according to community reporting on the episode.

The Laddu Janta Party

The campaign's organising genius was to treat six laddus with the full machinery of Indian politics. Students created an Instagram page called the Laddu Janta Party and filled it with memes, reels, slogans and protest videos. One placard, photographed and widely shared, did the arithmetic for the institute: "No Laddu = No Lecture."

The institute's explanation

Allen director Brajesh Maheshwari reportedly said the sudden increase in demand for sweets during the festive season had made it difficult to arrange enough halwais — traditional sweet-makers — to prepare the laddus within the required time. Community reporting on the protests said the founder moved to source sweets from confectioners in Jaipur and Indore at short notice. The institute reportedly began distributing laddus on November 5, following the protests. On Sunday, November 8, other coaching institutes in the city were said to have organised a bhandara — a community feast — offering sweets and food to students.

Why it landed

Strip away the jokes and the story is about what a festival sweet means to teenagers living away from home in a high-pressure coaching city: for many students, the box of laddus was the one piece of Diwali that Kota was going to give them before the train home. The protest was peaceful, funny and precisely targeted — and it worked on the timeline the students wanted, which is more than most protest movements in the city can say.
